hints: Focus on what makes a good preparation of an insoluble salt, a soluble barium compound followed by precipitation with sulfate.
Check route 1 first, Ba heated in oxygen gives BaO which dissolves in dilute HCl to give soluble BaCl2.
Test routes 2 and 3 the same way, see if each step gives only a soluble barium compound before H2SO4 is added so the final precipitate is pure BaSO4.
walkthrough:
**Recall the rule for pure insoluble salts**

A pure insoluble salt like $\text{BaSO}_4$ is best made by precipitation. Mix a soluble barium salt with dilute sulfuric acid, then filter, wash and dry.

$$\text{soluble Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s)$$

**Check route 1**

Ba metal in $\text{O}_2$ gives barium oxide, $\text{BaO}$. With dilute HCl this gives soluble $\text{BaCl}_2$.

$$\text{BaO} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{BaCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ 
Then $\text{BaCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4 + 2\text{HCl}$. Filtering gives pure $\text{BaSO}_4$, so 1 works.

**Check route 2**

Strong heating of $\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2$ gives solid $\text{BaO}$ by thermal decomposition.

$$2\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{BaO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$ 
In excess water this gives soluble $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$, which with $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ precipitates pure $\text{BaSO}_4$, so 2 works.

**Check route 3 and conclude**

$\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ gives soluble $\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2$.

$$\text{Ba(OH)}_2 + 2\text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{Ba(NO}_3)_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ 
Then with $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ it gives $\text{BaSO}_4$ precipitate, so 3 works. All three routes work.

options.A: Correct, because routes 1, 2 and 3 all produce a soluble barium compound (BaCl2, Ba(OH)2, Ba(NO3)2) before sulfate is added, so addition of dilute H2SO4 precipitates pure BaSO4 which can be filtered, washed and dried.
options.B: Incorrect. This omits route 3. Students sometimes think neutralisation to the nitrate introduces an impurity, but Ba(NO3)2 is fully soluble and reacts completely to give BaSO4 plus nitric acid which is washed away.
options.C: Incorrect. This omits route 1. Students sometimes worry that starting from a metal or forming BaO will contaminate the product, but BaO is converted fully to soluble BaCl2, leaving no insoluble impurity.
options.D: Incorrect. This suggests only one route works. The trap is thinking thermal decomposition of a Group 2 nitrate fails, but Ba(NO3)2 does decompose to BaO on strong heating, and BaO readily gives a soluble solution for precipitation.
